# Results -- Study 260 (Margin-Debt) on the real tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Recipe: at each
December year-end, compute the year-over-year change in NYSE/FINRA customer
margin debt; after a one-month reporting/execution lag (enter end-January of the
next year), measure the forward 12-month S&P 500 **price-only** return. Test the
contrarian claim that more leverage -> lower forward returns via (a) a HAC OLS
regression, (b) high/low YoY terciles, and (c) a fresh-record-high event test.
As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | Shape | Fingerprint (`fwd_ret`) |
|--------|--------|-------|-------------------------|
| FINRA/NYSE margin debt (Dec, hardcoded) x ^GSPC month-end (`_cache`, price-only) | 1960 -> 2024 | 65 forward-year observations | `3f24fa7a68df` |

Margin-debt levels are December snapshots (USD millions) hardcoded in `data.py`
(NYSE 1959-2009, FINRA 2010-2025). S&P 500 is `^GSPC_split_only` resampled to
month-end (split-adjusted, **dividends excluded**). For a contrarian "sell"
claim, dropping dividends is the *conservative* direction (it makes holding the
market look worse, which flatters the contrarian rule).

## Primary specification -- contrarian predictive regression

Forward 12m S&P price return regressed on standardized YoY margin growth:

| Quantity | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Slope (per +1 sigma of margin growth) | **-2.23%** forward return |
| HAC *t* on the slope | **-1.35** |
| R-squared | 0.023 |
| n (non-overlapping years) | 65 |

The slope has the **contrarian sign** the folklore predicts (more margin growth
-> lower forward return) but is **not significant**: |t| = 1.35 < 2. Margin
growth explains ~2% of the variance of next year's return.

## Extreme terciles -- surging vs contracting leverage

| YoY margin tercile | Mean forward 12m return | n |
|--------------------|------------------------|---|
| Bottom third (leverage contracting) | **+11.9%** | 22 |
| Middle third | +4.9% | 21 |
| Top third (leverage surging) | **+9.0%** | 22 |
| **High - Low spread** | **-2.9%** | -- |

High-minus-low Welch *t* = **-0.67**. The contrarian sign is there (surge years
trail contraction years) but the gap is small and statistically indistinguishable
from noise.

## The "record high" event test -- the literal newspaper headline

A 'record' year is one whose December margin debt set a fresh all-time high.

| Group | Mean forward 12m return | Up-rate | n |
|-------|------------------------|---------|---|
| Record-high years | **+6.6%** | 62.9% | 35 |
| Non-record years | **+11.1%** | -- | 30 |
| Unconditional | +9.x% | **73.9%** | 65 |
| Difference (record - non) | **-4.5%** | -- | -- |

Welch *t* = **-1.22** (p = 0.23). Record-margin-debt years *do* average a lower
forward return (+6.6% vs +11.1%) and a lower up-rate (62.9% vs the 73.9% base
rate) -- consistent with the famous post-record crashes of **2000 (-17%)**,
**2007 (-40%)**, and **2021 (-10%)** -- but with only 35 record-years and 17%
annual vol the difference does not clear the inference bar.

## Sub-period robustness -- the sign is stable, the significance never arrives

| Period | Slope | HAC *t* | n |
|--------|-------|---------|---|
| 1960--1989 | -2.67% | **-1.62** | 30 |
| 1990--2009 | -2.15% | -0.56 | 20 |
| 2010--2024 | -2.11% | -1.44 | 15 |

The contrarian slope is negative in **every** sub-period (a genuinely robust
*direction*), but never reaches |t| = 2. The effect is real-ish in sign and
hopeless in magnitude relative to the noise.

## Tradability -- the contrarian timing rule loses to buy-and-hold

Rule: go to cash for the 12 months following any year with margin-growth
z-score > +1.0 ("a surge"); otherwise hold the S&P. One-way cost 10 bps on NAV
per in/out switch.

| Strategy | Annualized (price-only) |
|----------|-------------------------|
| Buy-and-hold S&P (price-only) | **+7.53%/yr** |
| Contrarian timing rule (net of 10 bps) | **+6.51%/yr** |
| **Shortfall** | **-1.02 pp/yr** |

The rule sat in cash for 8 of 65 forward-years and *underperformed* buy-and-hold
by ~1pp/yr -- it dodged a few drawdowns but missed more up-years than it avoided
down-years. Adding dividends (a true total-return benchmark) widens the
shortfall further.

## Positive control -- the engine finds a contrarian signal when one exists

On the deterministic synthetic tape (`data.synthetic_series`, n=400) the same
regression recovers a planted forward contrarian relationship:

| Planted `predictive_beta` | Recovered slope | HAC *t* |
|---------------------------|-----------------|---------|
| 0.00 (null) | -0.004 | -0.57 |
| 0.03 | -0.043 | **-5.38** |
| 0.06 | -0.086 | **-11.0** |

The machinery is truthful: it reads ~zero on the null and strong-negative when a
real contrarian effect is planted. The real tape simply does not carry one strong
enough to clear |t| = 2.

## Verdict

- **Signal -- WEAK.** The contrarian sign is correct and stable across every
  sub-period (slope < 0 throughout; record-years average +6.6% vs +11.1%), and it
  rhymes with famous post-record crashes (2000, 2007, 2021). But the full-sample
  HAC *t* is only **-1.35**, the tercile *t* is **-0.67**, and the record-event
  *t* is **-1.22** -- nothing clears the |t| >= 2 bar. Literature/folklore support
  with a directionally-right-but-insignificant tape is **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability -- MIRAGE.** There is no tradable edge: the contrarian timing rule
  *underperforms* passive buy-and-hold by ~1pp/yr (price-only; worse on total
  return), because margin debt is a coincident, mechanical by-product of rising
  prices -- it goes up *because* the market went up, not before it falls.
- **Survivorship -- n/a.** Single index (S&P 500), no cross-sectional survivor
  selection. The honesty caveat here is the **price-only** return label, which is
  conservative for a contrarian claim.
